Motivation and history of Fubini's theorem It states that if a function is Lebesgue integrable on a rectangle  ${\displaystyle X\times Y}$ , then one can evaluate the double integral as an iterated integral y using an iterated integral. $${\displaystyle \,\iint \limits _{X\times Y}f(x,y)\,{\text{d}}(x,y)=\int _{X}\left(\int _{Y}f(x,y)\,{\text{d}}y\right){\text{d}}x=\int _{Y}\left(\int _{X}f(x,y)\,{\text{d}}x\right){\text{d}}y.}$$ A related theorem is often called Fubini's theorem for infinite series, although it is due to Alfred Pringsheim this theorem states that if  ${\textstyle \{a_{m,n}\}_{m=1,n=1}^{\infty }}$  is a double-indexed sequence of real numbers, and if  ${\textstyle \displaystyle \sum _{(m,n)\in \mathbb {N} \times \mathbb {N} }a_{m,n}}$  is absolutely convergent, then  ${\displaystyle \sum _{(m,n)\in \mathbb {N} \times \mathbb {N} }a_{m,n}=\sum _{m=1}^{\infty }\sum _{n=1}^{\infty }a_{m,n}=\sum _{n=1}^{\infty }\sum _{m=1}^{\infty }a_{m,n}}$  Although Fubini's theorem for infinite series is a special case of the more general Fubini's theorem, it is not necessarily appropriate to characterize the former as being proven by the latter because the properties of measures needed to prove Fubini's theorem proper, in particular subadditivity of measure, may be proven using Fubini's theorem for infinite series.
